A guide to tourism planning

Follow a tourism planning example across six steps. Open the dashboard links to explore the evidence, then return to this guide. Use Next, Previous or the arrow keys.

STEP 1 OF 6

Tourism planning with evidence

Attract visitors while understanding local impacts.

For tourism boards, destination managers and local government planners.

Explore: Overview ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Introduce the planning problem: visitor growth can bring spending, but a board also needs to understand timing and community impacts. Show the Overview page and explain that this is a selected national comparison, not a complete worldwide ranking. Use Croatia as the example throughout. The website frames questions for local investigation; it does not make investment decisions.

STEP 2 OF 6

Understand the dataset

16countries
96fields
2024tourism baseline

Missing means unavailable. Sources, definitions and years travel with each record.

Explore: Data & sources ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Open Data & sources. Search for Croatia and open its country brief to show a source link and metric definition. Explain that the original energy fields remain, tourism generally uses 2024 and airlines use 2023. Arrivals are trips with different national definitions; receipts are travel exports, not profit. Show the CSV download so an audience member can inspect the evidence themselves.

STEP 3 OF 6

Seasonal concentration differs

Share of annual accommodation nights in the two busiest months · 2024

Croatia 55.9%

France 36.0%

Germany 24.3%

Scale: 0–100%. Domestic and international guest nights. Eurostat.

Explore: Seasonal demand ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Open Seasonal demand. Keep Croatia as focus and select Germany as reference. Point to the monthly charts and expand Exact monthly values. Explain the two-busiest-month calculation and that monthly data are verified only for these three countries. Croatia’s concentration suggests investigating quieter months such as May or October. It does not demonstrate spare capacity or prove that visitors would shift their trips.

STEP 4 OF 6

Turn a pattern into local questions

A possible cultural-break pilot in a quieter month

  1. Compare national context.
  2. Review an illustrative attraction.
  3. Verify local accommodation and transport.
Explore: Attractions & transport ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Briefly open Compare countries and explain the up-to-four-country controls. Then open Attractions & transport and search Croatia. Dubrovnik’s Old City is an illustrative heritage example, not proof that Dubrovnik needs more visitors. Before choosing a destination or month, check opening dates, hotel availability and route schedules. National airline passengers cannot answer those access questions. Frame the campaign as a proposal subject to those checks.

STEP 5 OF 6

Community evidence is missing

1 / 16countries with a verified resident survey

Canada’s national result cannot establish support in Croatia or any specific community.

Review published, anonymized local evidence before scaling promotion.

Explore: Resident feedback ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Open Resident feedback with Croatia selected to show the explicit missing-data message. Use View verified Canada survey to demonstrate what sourced feedback looks like. Explain that 75% support continued promotion in that survey, not a generic satisfaction score. Do not transfer it to Croatia. Ask for existing aggregate local resident feedback and service-pressure measures. The website has no personal-data collection form.

STEP 6 OF 6

A proposal with clear limits

Pilot carefully. Measure locally. Keep uncertainty visible.

Test promotion outside Croatia’s peak only after local checks. Monitor visitor nights, service pressure and aggregate resident feedback.

National patterns and before-and-after changes do not prove causation.

Explore: Findings ↗
Walkthrough guidance

Open Findings and show both recommendations: investigate a seasonal pilot and require local community evidence before expanding promotion. Explain that measurement should account for weather, events and other changes, and check whether trips shifted from another month. Finish on Resources: point out the downloadable CSV, methodology summary and discussion of evidence limits. The main conclusion is that the site supports transparent planning questions, while local evidence is needed to justify action.
